ABSTRACT
A central idea in mechanistic interpretability is that neural networks represent more
features than they have dimensions, arranging them in superposition to form an
over-complete basis. This framing has been influential, motivating dictionary learn-
ing approaches such as sparse autoencoders. However, superposition has mostly
been studied in idealized settings where features are sparse and uncorrelated. In
these settings, superposition is typically understood as introducing interference
that must be minimized geometrically and filtered out by non-linearities such
as ReLUs, yielding local structures like regular polytopes. We show that this
account is incomplete for realistic data by introducing Bag-of-Words Superposi-
tion (BOWS), a controlled setting to encode binary bag-of-words representations
of internet text in superposition. Using BOWS, we find that when features are
correlated, interference can be constructive rather than just noise to be filtered
out. This is achieved by arranging features according to their co-activation pat-
terns, making interference between active features constructive, while still using
ReLUs to avoid false positives. We show that this kind of arrangement is more
prevalent in models trained with weight decay and naturally gives rise to seman-
tic clusters and cyclical structures which have been observed in real language
models yet were not explained by the standard picture of superposition. Code
for this paper can be found at: https://github.com/LucasPrietoAl/
correlations-feature-geometry.
1 INTRODUCTION
The field of mechanistic interpretability (MI) aims to understand deep learning models by decom-
posing them into interpretable components such as features or circuits, and understanding how these
interact (Olah et al., 2020). A central idea in this field is that models represent more features than they
have dimensions, arranging them in superposition to form an overcomplete basis (Elhage et al., 2022),
at the cost of allowing interference between features. This framing has been influential, motivating
dictionary learning approaches such as sparse autoencoders (SAEs), which can successfully recover
interpretable features from neural representations (Templeton et al., 2024; Gao et al., 2025).
While methods for finding features continue to advance, our understanding of how feature representa-
tions arrange themselves geometrically within high-dimensional activation spaces remains limited.
The geometry of features in superposition determines which concepts interfere with each other,
making it a key problem in MI (Sharkey et al., 2025) with implications for SAE training (Hindupur
et al., 2025), knowledge editing (Nishi et al., 2025), and adversarial robustness (Stevinson et al.,
2025; Gorton & Lewis, 2025). In existing toy models, superposition is typically understood as
introducing interference that should be minimized geometrically and filtered out with non-linearities
such as ReLUs (Elhage et al., 2022). This gives rise to arrangements such as regular polytopes, where
pairwise dot products are small and negative interference can be suppressed.
However, this perspective does not account for the kinds of structure observed in real language models.
Rather than local regular polytope structure, researchers have found ordered circles of features, such
as the months of the year (Engels et al., 2025), as well as anisotropic superposition, where related
features cluster together rather than minimizing dot products (Bricken et al., 2023; Templeton et al.,
2024). We argue that this discrepancy arises because realistic features are not sparse and uncorrelated.

To study this in a controlled setting, we introduce Bag-of-Words Superposition (BOWS), a framework
in which an autoencoder is trained to encode binary bag-of-words representations of internet text
in superposition. BOWS provides realistic feature correlations together with known ground-truth
features. Using this setup, we show that arranging features according to their co-activation patterns
naturally gives rise to semantic clusters and cyclical structures of the kind observed in real language
models. We refer to the regime in which low-rank structure in the data supports constructive
interference aslinear superposition.
Our main contributions are as follows:
• We introduce BOWS as a controlled setting to study superposition with realistic features.
•We show that, when features are correlated, interference can be constructive rather than only acting
as noise, and formalize a regime oflinear superpositionin which this constructive interference is
leveraged by non-linear AEs to enable efficient reconstruction in terms of weight norm and rank.
•We show that these solutions emerge prominently under tight bottlenecks or weight decay, and
that they reproduce key geometric structures observed in real language models, including semantic
clusters and cyclical structure.
•We introduce the distinction between presence-coding and value-coding features to explain the
existence of structured representations in the absence of feature correlations.

2.2 BOWS: REALISTIC DATA IN SUPERPOSITION
Studying superposition in the hidden representations of deep learning models requires postulating a

(BOWS), a setting for studying superposition with realistic feature correlations. Relative to the iid.
and pairwise-correlation settings considered in Elhage et al. (2022), BOWS induces richer covariance
structure, including approximately low-rank structure, while retaining known ground-truth features.

4 LINEAR SUPERPOSITION EXPLAINS FEATURE GEOMETRY IN REAL DATA
In Section 3, we argued that when features are correlated, interference need not be purely harmful:
it can also be constructive, allowing non-linear autoencoders to exploit low-rank structure in the
data rather than relying only on ReLU-based interference filtering. In this section, we show that this
mechanism accounts for the feature geometry observed in our main WikiText-BOWS setting.
Semantic clustering from constructive interference. A prominent observation in studies of LLM
activations is that learned features often form clusters based on semantic relatedness, leading to
anisotropic superposition, where features are not arranged to minimize pairwise dot products (Bricken
et al., 2023; Templeton et al., 2024). Such structure is difficult to reconcile with the standard picture
of superposition as purely harmful interference. By contrast, it arises naturally if a model exploits
constructive interference to capture low-rank structure in realistic data.
In Figure 3 we show UMAP (McInnes et al., 2018) projections of the word embeddings (columns of
W) learned by a ReLU AE trained on WikiText-BOWS ( V= 10,000 ) with varying latent dimensions
m. In panel (a), where compression is strong ( m= 200 ), we observe distinct clusters corresponding
to semantic categories (e.g. verbs, proper names, sports). This clustering weakens as the latent size
increases to m= 800 (Figure 3c), but reappears when weight decay is introduced (Figure 3d). These
results suggest that semantic clustering can arise as a consequence of constructive interference under
compression, and help explain why similar structure is observed in language models trained with
weight decay.
Cyclical structures inherited from data statistics. Another notable form of feature geometry
observed in real models is circular structure in the principal components of feature embeddings, for
concepts such as months of the year or days of the week (Engels et al., 2025).
Consider the features corresponding to the twelve months of the year. In Figure 4a, we show that
these features exhibit cyclic correlations in WikiText: for example, January co-occurs more often
with February and December than with August. This covariance structure drives the leading principal
components of the month activations, producing a circle in the 2D PCA plot in Figure 4b. Notably, the
learned latent representations exhibit the same geometry (Figure 4c). For a fully linear AE, this would

Furthermore, seasonal words such as ‘Christmas’ and ‘summer’ align with the months with which they
co-occur. This provides a direct example of correlated features being arranged so that interference
reflects shared structure in the data rather than being eliminated. We show as an example, that
interference from ‘December’ contributes to the reconstruction of ‘Christmas’ when they are both
present in the context, while interference from all the months almost cancels out and does not lead to
false positives when ‘Christmas’ is not present (Section 4). More detailed results for ‘Christmas’ and
other examples where interference is constructive are provided in Section C.

Constructive interference and interference filtering coexist in realistic data. In realistic data,
constructive interference and ReLU-based filtering can coexist within the same model, and even
for the same feature. This can be seen by comparing reconstruction in isolation and in context. If
interference were purely harmful, a feature would be reconstructed best in the one-hot setting, where
no other active features contribute interference. However, when a model exploits correlations between
features, the one-hot setting need not be optimal: correlated context can improve reconstruction by
contributing constructively to the target feature.
We observe exactly this phenomenon for words associated with The Beatles. These words are not
frequent enough to occupy nearly independent dimensions, yet ‘Beatles’ and the surnames of the
band members achieve validation R2values above 0.5while having near-zero one-hot R2. Thus,
interference from correlated words is not merely tolerated; it is beneficial. As shown in Figure 5
(middle), for 81% of validation samples containing ‘Beatles’, the contextual reconstruction is better
than the one-hot reconstruction. Figure 5 (right) shows the mechanism more directly: correlated
words provide positive evidence for the target word, while the ReLU and negative bias suppress false
positives when similar contexts occur without the target. This is precisely the realistic setting in
which constructive interference and interference filtering complement one another.
Word frequencies in natural text are highly heterogeneous (Zipf, 1949; Clauset et al., 2009), so
different features need not be represented by the same mechanism. Some can exploit correlation
structure and remain in linear superposition, while others are represented through stronger interference
filtering or become nearly orthogonal. Performing a linear superposition test on the m= 800 model
used in Figure 9, and using R= 0.5 as a threshold, we find that 4073 words are represented in
non-linear superposition, while the most frequent 522 words are represented in linear superposition.

5 VALUE-CODING FEATURES:GEOMETRY WITHOUT INPUT CORRELATIONS
While the BOWS framework can replicate the kind of semantic structure observed in the hidden
representations of language models, there are some examples, like the circles that appear in models
performing modular addition (Power et al., 2022; Nanda et al., 2023), which appear in the absence
of correlations in the data. To explain this kind of structure, we introduce the distinction between
value-codingandpresence-codingfeatures and explain how value-coding features can give rise to
apparent structures in features that are not actually represented in superposition.
Presence-coding features. We say that a representation h(x)∈Rdcontains apresence-coding
featureif some binary variable y(x) (e.g. “this token is the wordcat”) is recoverable by a linear
classifier. Formally, there exist weights {wk, bk}such that ˆy(x) = arg max k(w⊤
kh(x) +b k)predicts
y(x) with low error. Presence-coding features thus behave as detectors for discrete properties,
and different values of yare treated as separate classes without requiring any particular geometric
relation between them in representation spacea priori. For presence-coding features structured
representations are contingent on correlations in the data and capacity constraints that lead the
features to be represented in linear superposition.
Value-coding features. In contrast, we say that a representation h(x) contains avalue-coding feature
if a real-valued variable v(x)∈R (e.g. an angle, a coordinate, or a continuous latent factor) is linearly
decodable. That is, there exist w∈Rdandb∈R such that ˆv(x) =w⊤h(x) +b approximates
v(x) with low error. A collection of such value-coding features v1(x), . . . , v k(x)defines a low-
dimensionalvalue space Rk; plotting examples in this space can reveal semantically meaningful
structures (for instance, a 2D map from (x, y) coordinates, or a circle from (sinθ,cosθ) in modular
addition). Crucially, these structures are fully accounted for by the existence of linear value codes for
the underlying variables and therefore exist even in the absence of superposition.

Empirical evidence for value-coding features. To exemplify this, we look at a simplified modular
addition setup similar to that in Nanda et al. (2023), as well as a relative map position setup inspired
by Gurnee & Tegmark (2024). In the latter, we take the top 1,000 most populated cities in the US
and calculate their relative positions in terms of quadrants (e.g. Seattle is north-west of Denver).
The cities are embedded separately, fed through a 1-hidden layer ReLU MLP (details in Section A).
This latter dataset is designed to incentivize the model to learn 2 value-coding features encoding the
coordinates of each city since relative positions of the cities can easily be calculated by subtracting
coordinates. For both of these tasks, each integer or city pair only appears once across the train and
validation sets so no pair of cities or integers are correlated and we do not expect any kind of low
rank structure coming from linear superposition.
We validate that the cardinal direction model is learning value coding features for the coordinates
by training a linear probe to predict the coordinates of a subset of the cities from their embeddings.
We then use this probe to predict the coordinates of some held-out cities. The result is an average
R2validation score of 0.98 and a correct arrangement of the held out cities on the US map when
projected onto the directions identified by the linear probes (Figure 7). Similarly, we validate that the
relevant sine and cosine values are linearly represented by projecting the representations onto the
corresponding Fourier components in the case of modular addition (details in Section A).
We have shown two examples where neural networks need linearly represent values like coordinates
or trigonometric functions, in order to perform computations with them. We have then shown in
Figure 7 that in doing this, models implicitly create structures like circles or maps when we project
the data onto these value-coding features.

6 RELATED WORK
Superposition. Initial works in MI studied interpretable monosematic neurons in DL models Olah
et al. (2020); Cammarata et al. (2020) but faced challenges in interpreting polysemantic neurons
which activate for seemingly unrelated concepts. Elhage et al. (2022) introduced superposition as an
explanation for neuron polysemanticity. This view of DL models inspired further studies (Scherlis
et al., 2025) and sparse dictionary learning approaches like sparse autoencoders to decompose model
activations into an overcomplete basis of linear features (Gurnee et al., 2023; Huben et al., 2024;
Bricken et al., 2023). This approach has successfully been scaled to frontier language models and
multimodal models by Gao et al. (2025) and Templeton et al. (2024).

relations are encoded in language models while they show that categorical features which form

Lee et al. (2025) studied geometric similarities in token embeddings of different language models,
while Zhao et al. (2024) studied the kind of structure that emerges in the representations of models
trained on next token prediction. Li et al. (2025) showed that language models represent integers
in a helix structure to perform modular addition echoing the results from Nanda et al. (2023) and
Liu et al. (2022) on transformers trained for modular addition. Gurnee & Tegmark (2024) showed
that longitude and latitude as well as a notion of time, are encoded as linear features in language
models. The main results highlighted in this paper are circular structures formed by features and
semantic feature clusters, described in Engels et al. (2025) and Bricken et al. (2023) respectively.
These structures have also been studied as feature manifolds in Modell et al. (2025), and Hindupur
et al. (2025) highlighted the importance of understanding feature geometry when designing SAEs.
These findings sparked a discussion around the potential limitations of SDL approaches and the LRH
suggested by this non-linearly encoded semantic information (Sharkey et al., 2025).
Structure in word representations. Classic work on distributional semantics and word embeddings
(e.g., Word2Vec (Mikolov et al., 2013), GloVe (Pennington et al., 2014)) demonstrated that training
simple models on large text corpora leads to vector spaces where geometric relationships capture
surprisingly sophisticated semantic and syntactic relationships. Levy & Goldberg (2014) showed that
methods like Word2Vec with negative sampling implicitly factorize the Pointwise Mutual Information
(PMI) matrix shifted by a constant, while others show connections to PCA or SVD on co-occurrence
counts or PMI (Allen & Hospedales, 2019).
7 DISCUSSION& CONCLUSION
We introduced BOWS as a controlled setting for studying superposition with realistic feature correla-
tions. Our main result is that, when features are correlated, superposition does not only introduce
harmful interference to be filtered out: it can also exploit constructive interference, arranging features
according to their co-activation patterns. This mechanism yields norm- and rank-efficient reconstruc-
tions and accounts for semantic clusters and cyclical structures of the kind observed in real language
models (Bricken et al., 2023; Engels et al., 2025). We show this both in synthetic settings and in
realistic internet text, and find that such solutions are especially prevalent under tight bottlenecks and
weight decay. Finally, we distinguish these correlation-driven structures from value-coding feature
manifolds, which arise for functional reasons.
Limitations and future work. BOWS is intentionally simple, and does not capture the full richness
of language model representations. Our results show that constructive interference and ReLU-based
interference filtering can coexist, but we do not yet provide a complete mathematical characterization
of when each mechanism dominates. Important directions for future work include extending the
analysis to untied autoencoders and more realistic representation settings, and using BOWS as a
benchmark for SAE evaluation with known ground-truth feature geometry.

and integers could have a size-coding component as well as sine and cosine coding components which combine
to make a helix structure.

structure.title: Preface
structure.summary:
This partial document discusses the concept of "superposition" in neural networks, where models represent more features than their dimensions, leading to an over-complete basis. The authors argue that previous studies of superposition have focused on idealized, uncorrelated features, leading to the idea that interference between features is always detrimental and needs to be filtered out by non-linearities like ReLUs.

The paper introduces a new framework called "Bag-of-Words Superposition" (BOWS) to study superposition in more realistic settings with correlated features, using binary bag-of-words representations of internet text. Through BOWS, they demonstrate that when features are correlated, interference can be constructive, aiding in efficient reconstruction. This constructive interference, combined with ReLU filtering, can lead to semantic clusters and cyclical structures observed in real language models, which are not explained by the standard view of superposition. The authors also formalize a regime of "linear superposition" where this constructive interference is leveraged.

Key contributions highlighted include:
*   Introduction of BOWS for studying superposition with realistic features.
*   Demonstration that correlated features can lead to constructive interference, formalizing "linear superposition."
*   Showing that these structured representations emerge under conditions like weight decay and reproduce observed structures in language models.
*   Distinguishing between "presence-coding" and "value-coding" features to explain structured representations even without feature correlations.

structure.title: BACKGROUND:
structure.summary:
This document introduces a new framework called Bag-of-Words Superposition (BOWS) to study feature superposition in realistic data. The main points covered are:

*   **BOWS Framework:** A novel framework for studying superposition in autoencoders trained on binary bag-of-words representations of internet text, providing realistic feature correlations and known ground-truth features.
*   **Constructive Interference:** Demonstrates that in non-linear autoencoders, correlated features can lead to constructive interference, where shared variance reinforces signal rather than acting solely as noise. This is formalized as "linear superposition."
*   **Conditions for Linear Superposition:** Identifies conditions that favor linear superposition, including correlated features, a vocabulary size much larger than the latent dimension, weight decay, high sparsity (features rarely co-occurring), and uncorrelated features.
*   **Mechanisms of Interference Handling:** Distinguishes between interference as noise requiring non-linear filtering (e.g., ReLU) and constructive interference where features are arranged to reinforce each other, especially in low-rank data structures.
*   **Empirical Evidence in Non-linear AEs:** Shows that non-linear autoencoders, particularly with tight bottlenecks or weight decay, can exhibit linear superposition, leading to semantic clusters and cyclical structures observed in real language models.
*   **Value-Coding vs. Presence-Coding Features:** Introduces a distinction between presence-coding features (detectors for discrete properties) and value-coding features (linearly decodable real-valued variables), explaining how the latter can create structured representations even without input correlations.
*   **Heterogeneity of Feature Representation:** Highlights that different groups of features within a model can exhibit different structures (e.g., linear vs. non-linear superposition) depending on their frequency and correlation patterns.
*   **Complementarity of Mechanisms:** Argues that constructive interference and interference filtering can coexist within the same model, with correlated contexts improving reconstruction while non-linearities suppress false positives.

nodes.title: DEFINITIONS:
nodes.summary:
This partial document, published as a conference paper at ICLR 2026, focuses on empirical evidence for value-coding features in neural networks. The main points covered are:

*   **Demonstration of Value-Coding Features:** The paper presents experiments using simplified modular addition and relative map position setups to show that neural networks learn to represent specific values (like coordinates or trigonometric functions) as "value-coding features."
*   **Validation of Value-Coding:** Linear probes are used to predict coordinates from city embeddings and to validate the linear representation of sine and cosine values in modular addition. High R2 scores and accurate map reconstructions are reported.
*   **Ablation Studies:** Experiments involving ablating the value-coding subspace and its orthogonal complement demonstrate that the value-coding features are crucial for task performance, while other dimensions are less critical.
*   **Distinguishing Feature Geometry and Manifolds:** The paper proposes a method to differentiate between correlation-driven feature geometry (like semantic clusters) and task-driven value-coding feature manifolds, emphasizing that the latter arises from functional necessity.
*   **Related Work:** The document situates its findings within existing research on superposition, feature geometry, and structure in word representations, referencing numerous prior works.
*   **Implementation Details:** Specific details about datasets (WikiText-BOWS, synthetic months, modular addition, relative map positions), model architectures (MLPs, transformers), training procedures, and evaluation methods (linear probes, FEV) are provided in the appendix.
*   **Reproducibility:** The authors state that code to reproduce the main results is included in the supplementary material.

This document discusses the concept of "superposition" in deep learning models, particularly in the context of mechanistic interpretability. nodes.title: SUPERPOSITION AND INTERFERENCE
nodes.summary:
This partial document, published as a conference paper at ICLR 2026, discusses how autoencoders (AEs) can handle interference in data. The main points covered are:

*   **Two ways of handling interference:** The document contrasts two mechanisms:
    *   **Interference as noise:** This is the standard view where interference is filtered out by non-linearities like ReLU, especially when features are weakly correlated.
    *   **Constructive interference:** This occurs when the data covariance matrix has low rank, allowing interference to align with the signal and aid reconstruction. This is particularly effective in linear AEs and can also be leveraged by non-linear AEs under certain conditions.

*   **Mathematical formulation of reconstruction:** The reconstruction of a feature is decomposed into a "signal" term and an "interference" term, with the latter being the sum of dot products with other features' weights.

*   **Conditions favoring constructive interference:** This mechanism is favored when the rank of the feature covariance matrix is less than or equal to the latent size ($m$) of the AE.

*   **Linear AEs and PCA:** For linear AEs, the optimal learned mapping is equivalent to projecting onto the top $m$ principal components of the data covariance.

*   **Real-world data and approximate low-rank structure:** In real-world scenarios, covariance is often approximately low-rank, making constructive interference increasingly effective as the dominant components capture most of the variance.

*   **Non-linear AEs and weight decay:** The document explores when non-linear models, particularly those trained with weight decay, exploit constructive interference. Tight bottlenecks ($m \ll d$) combined with weight decay bias these models towards solutions that leverage low-rank structure.

*   **Complementarity of mechanisms:** The constructive and filtering mechanisms are not mutually exclusive and can coexist. A ReLU can suppress residual interference while the weight geometry exploits correlation structure.

*   **Empirical evidence:** The document presents empirical analysis using synthetic data with cyclic covariance and UMAP projections of word embeddings to demonstrate the emergence of linear superposition in non-linear AEs, showing how they can leverage constructive interference or form antipodal pairs depending on the latent size and training conditions.

*   **Implementation Details:**
    *   **WikiText-BOWS:** Specifies training parameters like learning rate, epochs, and batch size for models on this dataset.
    *   **Synthetic "Months" Dataset:** Describes a method for generating a synthetic dataset where documents are 12-bit vectors representing months, incorporating Gaussian blur and projection onto month directions to create a rank-2 correlation structure.
    *   **Modular Addition:** Outlines the architecture and training process for a model performing addition modulo 113, using embeddings and an MLP.
    *   **Relative Map Positions:** Details the setup for predicting relative city positions on a US map using embeddings and an MLP, drawing from the Cities1000 Dataset.
    *   **UMAP Plots and Semantic Clusters:** Explains how categories for UMAP plots were generated (using Gemini 2.5 Pro and manual refinement) and the parameters used for UMAP visualization.
    *   **Linear Probes:** Introduces the concept of linear probes to quantify the linearity of learned representations from ReLU-Autoencoders, defining metrics like Fraction of Explained Variance (FEV).

*   **ToyTransformer Setting:**
    *   Describes the training of a two-layer transformer on WikiText-103 for a multi-task token-recovery task.
    *   Details the transformer's architecture (embedding dimension, attention heads, MLP width, normalization).
    *   Explains the data and tokenization process for WikiText-103.
    *   Defines the target as a multi-hot vector indicating token presence in the prefix.
    *   Specifies the loss function (binary cross-entropy) and optimization details (AdamW, learning rate, weight decay, batch size, gradient clipping).
    *   Notes that semantic clusters and circular structures emerge in the transformer's residual stream, similar to the BOWS setup.

    *   Discusses how realistic models can leverage both constructive contributions from correlated features and suppression of false positives by ReLU and negative bias.

nodes.title: TOYTRANSFORMER SETTING
nodes.summary:
This partial document describes experiments with a two-layer transformer model trained on the WikiText-103 dataset for a multi-task token-recovery task. The main points covered are:

*   **Experimental Setup (TOYTRANSFORMER SETTING):**
    *   The model is a two-layer transformer.
    *   It's trained on WikiText-103.
    *   The task is to predict, at each position, the set of vocabulary items that have appeared in the causal context.
    *   The architecture includes pre-norm attention, MLP, and learned positional embeddings.
    *   Data is word-level tokenized with a fixed vocabulary.
    *   Targets are multi-hot vectors indicating token presence in the prefix.
    *   Training uses binary cross-entropy loss, AdamW optimizer, and specific hyperparameters.
*   **Results and Observations:**
    *   The transformer exhibits semantic clusters and ordered circular representations for months of the year, similar to previous findings.
    *   These semantic structures emerge in the residual stream as a byproduct of compression.
    *   UMAP and PCA are used to visualize these embeddings and weights, showing distinct clusters for various semantic categories.
*   **Combining Mechanisms (COMBINING CONSTRUCTIVE INTERFERENCE AND INTERFERENCE):**
    *   This section discusses how realistic models can combine multiple mechanisms.
    *   Correlated features can constructively contribute to reconstruction.
    *   ReLU and negative bias suppress false positives.
    *   An example with the word 'Christmas' illustrates how a feature might be partially reconstructable in isolation but benefits from combined mechanisms.

structure.title: CONSTRUCTIVE INTERFERENCE IN NON-LINEAR AES:
structure.summary:
This partial document, published as a conference paper at ICLR 2026, explores various aspects of transformer models and autoencoders, focusing on their ability to learn and represent semantic structures in data. Key points covered include:

*   **Transformer Model Training and Semantic Representation:** The document details the training of a two-layer transformer on WikiText-103 for a multi-task token-recovery task. It highlights the emergence of semantic clusters and ordered circular representations for months of the year in the model's internal representations (UMAP and PCA of embeddings and weights), replicating findings from previous work.
*   **Combining Constructive Interference and Interference Filtering:** This section investigates how realistic models can leverage both correlated features for constructive reconstruction and mechanisms like ReLU and negative bias to suppress false positives. It uses examples like "Christmas" and "mbar" to illustrate how related words contribute to better reconstruction, even when the target word is in an unusual context. The role of weight decay in favoring solutions that exploit shared low-rank structure is also discussed.
*   **PCA and Geometry Preservation:** The document explains how Pearson correlation coefficients induce Euclidean geometry on embedded points, making PCA equivalent to classical Multidimensional Scaling (MDS). This implies that PCA on correlation matrices yields embeddings that reflect the underlying data geometry.
*   **Replication on OpenWebText:** The main results regarding semantic clusters and circular representations for months are replicated on the OpenWebText dataset using a BOWS setup, demonstrating the generalizability of these findings.
*   **Weight Decay and Superposition:** The benefits of weight decay are further explored, showing that it helps maintain visible semantic structure across a broader range of latent sizes in autoencoders.
*   **Detailed Feature Geometry and Beyond 2D Structures:** The document provides extended visualizations of feature structures for various latent sizes, revealing rich sub-groupings within high-level semantic clusters (e.g., within "sciences"). It also presents 3D PCA examples for months and days of the week, indicating that their structures extend beyond a simple 2D circle.
*   **Correlation Structures in Synthetic Data:** The document examines superposition patterns in synthetic data with different correlation structures (figure-of-eight and spherical), showing how autoencoders leverage non-linear superposition at larger latent sizes, leading to sparse interference patterns.

This partial document, published as a conference paper at ICLR 2026, delves into the geometric structure of learned representations in autoencoders. Key points covered include:

*   **Visualizations of Latent Space Geometry:** Figure 13 shows reconstructions at various latent-vector sizes for different datasets ("Months," "Roman numerals"), illustrating how the structure of representations changes with dimensionality.
*   **Detailed Examination of Feature Geometry:** The document elaborates on the "Groups of Feature Geometry" (GMORE DETAILED EXAMPLE), providing extended analysis of feature structures across a range of latent sizes, building upon previous figures.
*   **Hierarchical Clustering within Representations:** Figure 16 highlights a zoomed-in UMAP plot, demonstrating that within broader semantic clusters (e.g., "sciences"), finer sub-clusters exist (e.g., medicine, astronomy, chemistry, biology). This indicates a rich, non-trivial geometric organization.
*   **Beyond 2D Representations:** Section G.1 ("SOME EXAMPLES BEYOND2D") discusses how temporal concepts like days of the week and months of the year exhibit structure beyond a simple 2D circular arrangement, with an "ondulation" in the third principal component for months. Figure 14 visualizes this 3D PCA.
*   **Correlation Structures in Synthetic Data:** Section H ("OTHER CORRELATION STRUCTURES IN SYNTHETIC DATA") explores how autoencoders trained on data with different correlation structures (circular, figure-of-eight, spherical) exhibit distinct weight patterns. Figure 15 extends previous analysis to more latent sizes and these new correlation structures, comparing linear and ReLU autoencoders.
*   **Partial Reconstruction and Semantic Meaning:** Section I ("A TAIL OF PARTIALLY RECONSTRUCTED FEATURES") argues that meaningful geometry in representations does not always equate to accurate reconstruction. Features can occupy correct semantic regions due to shared directions with correlated features, even if their individual variance is not well captured. This is illustrated with Figure 16 again, emphasizing that semantic organization can precede accurate feature-level recovery.
*   **Implications for the Linear Representation Hypothesis (LRH):** Section J ("IMPLICATIONS FOR THE LINEAR REPRESENTATION HYPOTHESIS") discusses the ongoing debate and different formulations of the LRH within mechanistic interpretability, touching upon its meaning in terms of one-dimensional directions and mathematical linearity.

The partial document discusses the geometric organization of features in a model's latent space, particularly in the context of autoencoders. It presents findings from a conference paper published at ICLR 2026. Key points include:

*   **Geometric Structure and Reconstruction Accuracy:** The document highlights that meaningful geometric relationships between features in the latent space do not necessarily imply accurate individual feature reconstruction. Models with limited capacity might place features in semantically correct regions by projecting them onto shared directions used by correlated features, even if their individual variance is not well captured.
*   **"Best Guess" Representation:** This phenomenon suggests that semantically meaningful geometry can reflect a "best guess" induced by surrounding features rather than a precise representation of a concept itself.
*   **Sub-clusters and Data Statistics:** Even with poor reconstruction scores, features can form semantic clusters. This is explained by the autoencoder learning a low-rank representation of dominant co-activation structures, projecting many features onto a shared subspace. These features then inherit meaningful geometry from data statistics.
*   **Example of Science Features:** Figure 16 illustrates this with science-related features, showing distinct sub-clusters for medicine, astronomy, and chemistry within a broader science region, even when individual features are partially reconstructed. This indicates that the model learns relative feature positioning before achieving accurate individual reconstruction.
*   **Implications for Linear Representation Hypothesis (LRH):** The document touches upon the Linear Representation Hypothesis, a foundational concept in mechanistic interpretability. It notes the lack of consensus on its precise formulation, mentioning interpretations related to one-dimensional directions in activation space and mathematical linearity (additivity and scaling of representations).

structure.title: IMPLICATIONS FOR THE LINEAR REPRESENTATION HYPOTHESIS
structure.summary:
This partial document, published as a conference paper at ICLR 2026, discusses findings related to the geometry of learned representations in deep learning models. Key points include:

*   **Feature Geometry and Reconstruction:** The document explores the relationship between the geometric arrangement of features in a latent space and their reconstruction accuracy. It suggests that meaningful geometry can emerge even when features are not accurately reconstructed, implying that models might leverage shared directions from correlated features to place them in semantically relevant regions.
*   **Low-Rank Representation and Data Statistics:** The paper posits that autoencoders can learn low-rank representations of dominant co-activation structures in data. This allows them to project many features, even less common ones, onto a shared subspace, inheriting meaningful geometry from data statistics without necessarily achieving accurate feature-level reconstruction.
*   **UMAP Visualization and Sub-clusters:** Figure 16 illustrates this with a zoomed-in UMAP plot, showing distinct sub-clusters for medical, astronomical, and chemical features within a broader "science" region, even for partially reconstructed features. This indicates that the model learns relative feature positioning before achieving individual accuracy.
*   **Linear Representation Hypothesis (LRH):** The document delves into the implications for the LRH, a foundational concept in mechanistic interpretability. It discusses different formulations of the LRH and argues that observed geometric structures like ordered circles do not necessarily undermine either formulation.
*   **Value-Coding vs. Presence-Coding Features:** The paper introduces the concept of "value-coding" features, which encode concrete trigonometric values or coordinates along linear directions. It suggests that these features might conflict with the mathematical linearity aspect of the LRH, as scaling their value can lead to different, potentially invalid, trigonometric values.
*   **Dimensionality Reduction Method Independence:** Figure 18 demonstrates that the observed semantic clustering results are consistent across different dimensionality reduction techniques, including UMAP, t-SNE, and PaCMAP, suggesting the robustness of the findings.

structure.summary: This partial document, published as a conference paper at ICLR 2026, discusses the interpretation of feature geometry in deep learning models. It presents UMAP embeddings at various latent-vector sizes, showing that semantic clusters persist even when filtering features based on their R2 values. The paper argues that observed feature structures, such as ordered circles formed by months, can arise from the compression and reconstruction of one-dimensionally linear features, and thus do not necessarily invalidate existing definitions of linear representation hypotheses (LRH). However, it also suggests that some features might be "value-coding," encoding concrete trigonometric values or coordinates along linear directions, which could conflict with the constraints of mathematical linearity. The document proposes exploring the possibility of presence-coding features having value-coding components, drawing parallels to city representations in language models and integer projections onto helix subspaces. Ultimately, the findings suggest that complex feature geometry can often be explained by linear superposition, but the existence of value-coding features may represent an exception or conflict with mathematical linearity. The paper also includes a section on other dimensionality reduction methods (t-SNE and PaCMAP) to demonstrate that the observed semantic clustering is independent of the chosen technique.
